# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand features a well-established system that includes early childhood, primary, secondary, and tertiary education. Early childhood education is available in various settings such as kindergartens, kōhanga reo (Māori immersion), and playcentres, with a strong emphasis on qualified teaching staff. Primary and secondary education is free and compulsory from ages 6 to 16, though most children start at age 5 and remain enrolled until at least 17. The school year is divided into four terms, and students progress through Years 1–13, transitioning to secondary school at around age 13. The national curriculum (New Zealand Curriculum for English-medium and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa for Māori-medium schools) covers multiple learning areas, with core subjects compulsory until Year 10. From Year 11, students pursue the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) or may opt for international qualifications like Cambridge or IB.
New Zealand’s education system includes state (public), state-integrated, and private schools. State schools follow a secular curriculum and are free for citizens and residents, though voluntary donations and fees for extras are common. State-integrated schools retain a "special character" (often religious) and charge compulsory attendance dues, while private schools rely mainly on tuition fees. Māori language and Māori-medium pathways have expanded since the 1980s, with options ranging from full immersion (kura kaupapa Māori) to Māori language subjects in mainstream schools. Manual and technical education is integrated into the curriculum, and tertiary education encompasses universities, polytechnics, and other providers, with funding support available through student loans and allowances. The government provides targeted resources for low-decile schools, special needs students, and recognizes the significant achievement gap between Māori/Pacific and Pākehā students. Education in New Zealand is characterized by local school boards, government oversight, and ongoing efforts to improve standards and equity.
